primer.text: From the Momentum subtopic you already know how to compute momentum as mass multiplied by velocity, and from earlier in Forces & Motion you know that a resultant force changes an object's velocity. This note joins the two ideas: a resultant force acting on a moving object changes that object's momentum, and how quickly the change happens decides how large the force must be.

modules.title: Forces & momentum
modules.opening: Push a moving trolley and it speeds up; drag your feet on it and it slows down. Either way its momentum changes, and this lesson turns that observation into the syllabus equation: force equals change in momentum divided by time. You will also learn the symbol-by-symbol anatomy of F = (mv − mu)/t and the sign rule that keeps rebound questions honest.
keyPoints: A resultant force on a moving object changes its velocity — speeding it up or slowing it down — and so changes the object's momentum.
Combining F = ma with p = mv gives F = (mv − mu)/t: force equals change in momentum divided by the time taken.
In the equation, m is mass in kilograms, u the initial velocity, v the final velocity and t the time in seconds.
A momentum change is quoted in kg m/s, and the force that causes it in newtons (N).
Choose one direction as positive before substituting: motion the opposite way enters the equation as a negative value.

low.restatement: A force that speeds an object up or slows it down is changing its momentum, and the force equals that momentum change divided by the time taken.
low.analogy: Momentum is the cargo of motion in a trolley; a force is the hand loading or unloading it, and time is how long the hand gets to work.
low.examPointer: When a question names the relationship, write F = (mv − mu)/t in full — marks sit in the formula as well as in the final number.

medium.restatement: The equation is a double substitution: p = mv turned into before-and-after values (mu and mv), then fed into F = ma with a = (v − u)/t.
medium.analogy: Treat momentum like a bank balance: mu is the opening balance, mv the closing balance, and force the payment rate moving money between them during time t.
medium.examPointer: Sign discipline earns the marks: fix the initial direction as positive and carry every minus through mv − mu before you divide.

modules.title: Rate of change in momentum
modules.opening: A change of momentum can arrive gently or with a bang, and the only difference is time. Divide the same change by a long contact time and the force is tame; divide it by a blink and the force is brutal. This lesson reads the equation as a rate, then follows two worked collisions — a ball on a racket and a car on a wall.
keyPoints: Force is the momentum change per second — the rate at which a body's momentum changes.
Squeezing a momentum change into a shorter time makes the force bigger.
Force and contact time are inversely proportional: doubling the time halves the force, and halving the time doubles it.
The same 0.5 kg m/s momentum change delivers 0.25 N over 2.0 s but 5.0 N over just 0.1 s.
A car rebounding from a wall carries a negative final velocity, so the calculated force comes out negative — opposite to its initial motion.

low.restatement: The same momentum change divided by a shorter time gives a bigger force — force and time pull in opposite directions.
low.analogy: Catch an egg with stiff arms and it stops instantly and splats; let your hands drift back and the longer stop softens the force.
low.examPointer: When a question doubles or halves the contact time at fixed momentum change, answer with the inverse move: halve or double the force.

medium.restatement: Force as a rate means how much momentum changes each second, not how much changes in total.
medium.analogy: A fixed momentum change is a fixed journey; contact time is the pace you travel it, and rushing the journey spikes the force.
medium.examPointer: Airbags, seatbelts and crumple zones are this law in disguise: they stretch the contact time to cut the peak force.

glossary.definition: The quantity a moving object carries because of its motion: mass multiplied by velocity, with units of kg m/s.
Final momentum minus initial momentum (mv − mu); the quantity that a force acting over a time alters.
The single overall force on an object; it appears in both F = ma and the momentum equation.
How much a quantity changes per unit time; force is the momentum change per second.
Paired so that multiplying one quantity by a factor divides the other by the same factor.
The duration for which a striking object and the surface it strikes stay in touch.

workedExample.prompt: A 1500 kg car runs into a wall while moving at 15 m/s and bounces straight back at 5 m/s; the impact lasts 3 s. Calculate the average force on the car and state which way it acts.
steps: Take the initial direction as positive, so the rebound velocity is v = −5 m/s, and list the knowns: m = 1500 kg, u = 15 m/s, t = 3 s.
Write the relationship: F = (mv − mu)/t, the momentum change divided by the contact time.
Momentum after: mv = 1500 × (−5) = −7500 kg m/s; momentum before: mu = 1500 × 15 = 22500 kg m/s.
Divide by the contact time: F = −30000 / 3 = −10000 N.
workedExample.finalAnswer: F = −10000 N — a 10000 N force acting opposite to the car's original direction of travel.
